title: Australian Baby First in World to Receive Precision Treatment for Rare Epilepsy
excerpt: Eight-month-old Bodhi went from 50 seizures a day to virtually none within weeks, while Indian doctors advance VNS therapy for drug-resistant cases.
body:
• Eight-month-old Bodhi from New South Wales became the first person in the world to receive a precision treatment for KCNT1-related epilepsy, reducing seizures from 50–60 daily to virtually zero
  • NSW Health’s new Innovative Therapies Pathway delivered the experimental treatment within six weeks of diagnosis
  • In Hyderabad, doctors at CARE Hospitals successfully used Vagus Nerve Stimulation to manage drug-resistant epilepsy, achieving significant seizure control and improved quality of life

An eight-month-old baby from New South Wales has become the first person in the world to receive a groundbreaking precision treatment for KCNT1-related epilepsy, a rare and often fatal genetic disorder that had left him suffering 50 to 60 seizures every day.

Bodhi Higginson was diagnosed with the condition after experiencing seizures at just three months old. Through NSW Health’s newly developed Innovative Therapies Pathway — a streamlined system for fast-tracking precision medicine for rare conditions — the Sydney Children’s Hospital Network identified the genetic mutation driving his epilepsy and matched it with an experimental treatment developed overseas.

A Dramatic Transformation

Bodhi received his first dose on April 21, 2026. Three days later, he had his final seizure. Within weeks, he began regaining developmental milestones that the relentless seizure activity had stalled.

KCNT1-related epilepsy affects an estimated 2,500 children in the United States alone. Mutations in the KCNT1 gene cause abnormal potassium flow through ion channels in the brain, triggering uncontrollable seizures that severely impair cognitive and motor development. Until now, no disease-modifying therapy existed.

The treatment was enabled by advances in precision medicine and clinical trial infrastructure. San Diego-based Actio Biosciences announced its first participant dosed in a Phase 1 clinical trial of ABS-1230, a KCNT1 inhibitor, in September 2025, with the U.S. FDA granting Fast Track designation. A Northwestern University study published in Nature Communications in April 2026 further demonstrated how RNA-based treatments could protect developing brains from KCNT1-driven hyper-excitation.

Hyderabad Doctors Advance VNS Therapy

In a parallel development, doctors at CARE Hospitals in Hyderabad’s Banjara Hills have successfully managed complex drug-resistant epilepsy using Vagus Nerve Stimulation, an FDA-approved therapy that delivers electrical impulses to the brain through a device implanted under the skin.

“Every patient with drug-resistant epilepsy deserves an individualised treatment plan. This case highlights the importance of timely referral, multidisciplinary care, and evidence-based advanced therapies in managing complex epilepsy.”

— Dr. Shashank Jaiswal, Consultant – Epilepsy & Neurology, CARE Hospitals, Hyderabad

Dr. Jaiswal’s team treated a patient whose seizure burden had been reduced by nearly 90% through optimized anti-seizure medications, but persistent focal seizures continued affecting daily life. Since conventional epilepsy surgery was not suitable, the team implanted a VNS device. The patient experienced remarkable improvement in seizure control, cognition, behavior, and overall independence.

What It Means for Patients

Both developments represent a shift toward individualized epilepsy care. Experts advise that patients who continue to have seizures despite trying two appropriate anti-seizure medications should seek evaluation at a specialized epilepsy center rather than relying solely on repeated medication changes. Early assessment can identify advanced options such as precision gene-targeted therapies, epilepsy surgery, or VNS — interventions that can significantly alter long-term outcomes.
